text: Sheath rot (ចំនួរលួយស្រទាប្9f្លិក, "chomngu roluy srotoap sleuk") is caused by the fungus Sarocladium oryzae. It develops on the flag leaf sheath - the sheath that wraps around the developing panicle - producing irregular brown-to-gray lesions on that sheath. Because the infected sheath doesn't open and expand normally, the panicle trapped inside is often unable to emerge fully: it may stay partly enclosed, come out twisted, or emerge deformed, resulting in poor grain fill and discolored grains. The source lists this alongside sheath blight as a late-season sheath disease that mainly damages yield and grain quality/appearance rather than killing the plant outright. Management follows the same logic as other sheath diseases: avoid overly dense planting and excess nitrogen (both raise humidity inside the canopy where this fungus thrives), use clean seed, and remove and destroy infected stubble and straw after harvest so spores don't carry over to the next crop.
